source.version: Journal version of record: The Journal of Creative Behavior, 2025; 59:e70022, https://doi.org/10.1002/jocb.70022 (received 15 October 2024, revised 2 April 2025, accepted 7 April 2025), open access copy from the University of Adelaide/UniSA repository
source.title_on_document: Human- AI Co- Creativity: Does ChatGPT Make Us More Creative?

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. Data Availability Statement (p. 8): 'Data available on request.'
supplement.holds: Nothing indicates statistics outside the main text. Per-arm analyzed counts for the DAT and per-contrast Tukey p-values are not printed anywhere in the PDF.

paper_design_summary: University students in the US Midwest were randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions in a 2 (prime source label: 'a student' vs 'ChatGPT') x 3 (prime creativity: low, typical, high) between-subjects design. Each participant saw one fixed list of seven nouns (an example Divergent Association Task response), retyped it, rated how creative it was, and then completed the DAT. The outcome is the participant's DAT score (semantic-distance score of their own word list); the same three word lists were used under both source labels.

studies.label: 2 x 3 priming experiment (prime source label x prime creativity) with DAT outcome

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of six priming conditions: the attributed source of a seven-noun example list ('a student' vs 'ChatGPT') crossed with the list's creativity level (low, typical, high). The word list is identical across the two source labels at each level; only the attribution differs.
assignment.quote: Participants responded to a set of demographic questions and a suite of personality, creativity, and AI covariates before being randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1 Design and Participants; p. 4, Section 3.2 Procedure and Section 3.3 Priming; Table 1 (p. 4)

participants.exclusions: Table 1 (p. 4) gives 387 people across the six conditions as the result of random allocation. Participants who failed an end-of-study attention check were removed (p. 4, Section 3.4), but the paper does not say how many, nor whether the 387 is counted before or after that removal. DAT score N = 381 (Table 3, p. 5; matches ANOVA F(5, 375)); the 6 missing DAT scores are not explained and per-arm DAT counts are not printed. Table 3 lists 'Total (valid)' N = 376; the hierarchical regression degrees of freedom (F(1, 376), F(6, 371)) imply 378 observations. The perceived-creativity ANOVA uses all 387 (F(5, 381)).
participants.who: Participants from an urban university in the Midwest of the United States; 107 male, 273 female, 6 non-binary/fluid/transgender, 1 declined; mean age 23.87
participants.quote: Participants (N = 387), drawn from an urban university in the Midwest of the United States, took part in a study using a 2 (Prime Source: Human vs. ChatGPT) x 3 (Prime Creativity: Low, Typical, High) factorial design.
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Table 1; p. 5, Table 3

ai_tool.name_model: Labeled 'ChatGPT'; no model or version named. The creativity levels of the lists were 'determined from a sample (Cropley 2023) of ChatGPT responses (N = 102)' (p. 4); the paper does not state clearly who produced each list.
ai_tool.how_used: No participant used an AI tool. Each participant saw one fixed seven-noun example DAT response, told it came from either 'a student' or 'ChatGPT', retyped it, rated its creativity on a 1-5 scale, and then did the DAT. Whether the list stayed visible while participants wrote their DAT words is not stated.

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): 'Please enter 10 words that are as different from each other as possible, in all meanings and uses of the words', with rules (single English nouns, no proper nouns, no specialized vocabulary, think of words on your own). Scored by semantic distance; reported as DAT score and DAT percentile rank.

outcomes.name: DAT score (verbal divergent ideation)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Association Task score (semantic distance among the participant's own nouns; Olson et al. 2021). Table 3: DAT score N = 381, min 61.16, max 94.45, mean 80.25, SD 6.30; DAT percentile rank N = 381, mean 60.28, SD 27.59. Analyzed by one-way ANOVA across six conditions with Tukey HSD post hoc tests (H1), and as the dependent variable in a hierarchical regression where the priming condition is entered at step 5 (H3). Coded with_ai because the AI-attributed example was presented within the same session immediately before the DAT; whether it remained visible during the DAT is not stated.

contrasts.reported: ChLo M = 76.37, SD = 5.71 vs HuLo M = 79.96, SD = 5.94; Tukey HSD: ChLo 'significantly different from all other conditions' (no per-contrast p printed). Omnibus F(5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.08. Allocation ns 53 vs 56 (Table 1); analyzed per-arm ns not printed. Figure 2 shows means with 95% CI. Source label differs; list content is identical.
ChTy M = 81.21, SD = 6.07 vs HuTy M = 79.74, SD = 7.24; only ChLo differed significantly in Tukey HSD. Allocation ns 74 vs 69 (Table 1).
ChHi M = 81.11, SD = 5.66 vs HuHi M = 82.18, SD = 5.63; only ChLo differed significantly in Tukey HSD. Allocation ns 68 vs 67 (Table 1).

eligibility.reason: People were randomly allocated to six priming conditions (p. 3-4), and 381 people have DAT scores (Table 3, p. 5), an automated creativity score of their own output. Criterion 1 is unclear: no one used an AI tool; the 'AI assistance' is a single fixed seven-noun example list labeled as from ChatGPT, and the comparison arms see the identical list labeled as from a student. The source contrast therefore isolates the AI label, not AI-generated content; the level contrast varies the example's creativity under either label. Review 1 should decide whether a label-only manipulation of a supplied example counts as random assignment to generative-AI assistance (ideas_supplied).

one_line_finding: DAT scores did not differ by prime source or level except that the low-creativity list labeled as from ChatGPT lowered scores (ChLo M = 76.37, SD 5.71 vs 79.74 to 82.18 in the other five conditions; F(5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.08; pp. 5-6, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
open_questions: Does a label-only manipulation (identical example list attributed to 'ChatGPT' vs 'a student') satisfy criterion 1? If yes, the ChatGPT-vs-student contrasts are ai_vs_active with identical content.
Setting not stated (in-person lab vs online survey); coded lab_rct for a university student sample.

Who produced each prime list is unclear. The text says levels were determined from a sample of ChatGPT responses, but the low list has PR = 0.05 (text, p. 4) or 0.03 (Table 2 header, p. 4), while the introduction reports GPT-4 percentile ranks in Cropley (2023) ranging from 31.03 to 99.60 (p. 2).
Whether the prime list stayed on screen during the DAT is not stated.
Per-arm analyzed ns for the DAT (total 381) are not printed; only allocation ns (Table 1, total 387) are given. Number removed by the attention check is not stated.
notes: Inconsistency: low-creativity prime PR = 0.05 in text (p. 4, Section 3.3) vs PR = 0.03 in the Table 2 header (p. 4). Inconsistency in sample counts: Table 3 'Total (valid)' N = 376 vs regression df implying 378. Outcome not listed because it is not scored on participants' output: perceived creativity of the prime (1-5 self-rating of the example list; F(5, 381) = 71.90, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.48; HuLo 1.91, ChLo 2.04, HuTy 4.16, HuHi 4.13, ChTy 3.73, ChHi 3.93; pp. 6-7, Section 4.2, Figure 3). Covariates (openness, creative self-efficacy, trust in AI, creative personal identity, AI familiarity) were measured before allocation. Ethics approval: University of Nebraska at Omaha IRB 0223-23-EX (p. 8).
